reader.title: Killing of Ike Kinney
bases: A posse of citizens hunting Kinney for two killings surrounded him in a river bottom and shot him dead after, by their account, he opened fire (A5, A2).

A group of about twenty-five citizens hunting Kinney as an accused murderer killed him, but every report describes a gunfight in which he fired first and wounded two posse members before W. C. Nash shot him, not a killing of a captured or helpless man (A5, A6); all accounts come from the posse's side, and no report states whether the posse acted under legal authority except the Ocala brief's 'sheriff's posse' (A4).

Nearly every report of the killing derives from one Lewisville special to the Arkansas Gazette (A5, A6, A12); the Stamps dispatches (A1, A2) cover only the earlier killings, and the Ocala brief (A4) agrees on the core event but looks like a garbled condensation rather than an independent report.

summary.text: The killing of Ike Kinney was the shooting of a Black man, Ike or Isaac Kinney, by a posse of citizens at Doella, six miles south of Lewisville, Arkansas, on August 3, 1905.

Kinney was hunted as the accused killer of a Black man at Stamps and of E. R. Ferguson, a railroad claim agent with a pursuing posse, and was reported to have wounded four more people before he was shot.
An Arkansas Gazette dispatch listing his "bloody record" ran in white papers across the country, and one Black weekly, the St. Louis Palladium, reprinted it.
According to a Stamps dispatch of August 2, Kinney killed a Black man at Stamps that morning and escaped.
A posse went after him, and about three miles from Stamps he opened fire on it and killed Ferguson, claim agent of the Louisiana and Arkansas railroad.
A $500 reward was offered, and special trains were sent to Pine Bluff to bring bloodhounds to Stamps.
At 3 a.m. on August 3, near Lewisville, Kinney was reported to have fired a Winchester at a couple named Stewart, of Greensburg, wounding both.
The Gazette's correspondent wrote that Kinney then told the couple he had taken them for members of a posse and was "very sorry that he had fired on them."
Later that morning about twenty-five men with dogs took up his trail, guided by a farmer who said a Black man had asked to be taken across the Red River.
Members of the search party found Kinney in a bottom near Doella, a plantation post office, and a posse left Lewisville shortly before noon on a special train.
When the posse closed in, Kinney opened fire, shooting a finger off C. F. Nash and wounding Alvin Barham through the neck, and W. C. Nash then shot him dead.
The posse and the body were carried back to Stamps on the special train, and the reward for Kinney's capture "dead or alive" had by then reached $1,500.
No report of an inquest, of any inquiry into the shooting, or of the fate of the wounded appears in the coverage.
The Gazette special, datelined Little Rock, August 3, ran the next day in the Louisville Courier-Journal, the Montgomery Advertiser and the Richmond Times-Dispatch.
The New-York Tribune, the Los Angeles Herald and the St. Louis Republic carried it the same day.
Headlines cast Kinney as a criminal type: the Courier-Journal ran "Bloody Record Made By a Bad Negro In Arkansas," and the Montgomery Advertiser "Bad Negro Is Slain."
Other papers called him a "Wild Man" or a "Negro Terrorist" who "Dies in True Bandit Style," the last in the Daily Ardmoreite of August 6.
Weeklies such as the Spanish Fork Press in Utah reprinted it the next week as "Ike Kinney Put to Death by Posse."

The only Black-press item found, in the St. Louis Palladium of August 5, reprinted the opening of the Gazette dispatch under the deck "If Reports of His Doings Are Correct He Was Not Suppressed Any Too Soon."
That headline endorsed the killing if the reports were true; the paper added no reporting of its own, and no version in either press gave an account from Kinney's side.

Garbled versions also circulated: the Ocala Evening Star's one-sentence item named the man "Black Tracy" and placed the killing near "Louisville, Ark.," and an East Oregonian brief called him "a Louisville, Kan., negro."

The man's name appears as "Ike Kinney" in most Gazette and Associated Press versions, "Isaac Kinney" in others, "Guy Kinney" in a special to the Daily Sentinel, and "Black Tracy" in the Ocala Evening Star.
The Ocala brief also credited a sheriff's posse and counted five people shot, two fatally, where the Lewisville dispatch described a posse of citizens and itemized six people shot.
The Lewisville dispatch, written near the scene and naming the man who fired the fatal shot, is the more detailed source on these points.

accounts.label: Gazette special from Lewisville (posse's account)
accounts.gist: Kinney left a 'bloody record' of two killed and four shot in twenty-four hours; tracked by men with dogs, he fired on the posse that surrounded him at Doella and was shot dead by W. C. Nash.

accounts.label: Stamps dispatches
accounts.gist: Kinney killed a Black man at Stamps, fled, and killed Ferguson of the pursuing posse; a reward was offered and bloodhounds sent for.

accounts.label: Ocala brief
accounts.gist: 'Black Tracy', who had shot five persons, two fatally, in ten days, was killed near Louisville, Ark., by a sheriff's posse.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Bloody Record Made By a Bad Negro In Arkansas' and 'Bad Negro Is Slain' presented the killing as the end of a desperado's rampage, from the posse's side only.
Later reprints called him a 'Wild Man' and a 'Negro Terrorist' who 'Dies in True Bandit Style'.
The Ocala Evening Star ran a one-sentence brief, 'Negro Desperado Killed', with a different name and place.
The St. Louis Palladium reprinted the wire under 'If Reports of His Doings Are Correct He Was Not Suppressed Any Too Soon', approving the killing conditionally on the reports' accuracy.

conflicts.note: The Gazette and AP versions agree on Kinney; 'Black Tracy' appears only in the Ocala brief.

Ike Kinney (also 'Isaac Kinney', 'Guy Kinney', and 'Black Tracy'), described as 'a desperate negro'
Accused of killing a Black man at Stamps and E. R. Ferguson, a member of a pursuing posse, on August 2, and of shooting Mr. and Mrs. Stewart, Alvin Barham and C. F. Nash
A posse of citizens from Lewisville, arriving by special train; W. C. Nash fired the fatal shot (Ocala brief: a sheriff's posse)
Kinney, killed by the posse; also an unnamed Black man at Stamps whom Kinney was accused of killing on August 2
The posse and the body were taken back to Stamps on a special train
